subject: General Tips
title: Syncope: Cardiac vs Neurological vs Vasovagal
preview: Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness related to cerebral hypoperfusion; triggers, prodrome, exertional symptoms and cardiac findings guide risk.

sections.title: Start with red flags
points: Evaluate chest pain, palpitations, known heart disease, family history of sudden death, exertional collapse and abnormal ECG.
Check vital signs and other emergency causes when history suggests instability.

sections.title: Compare common mechanisms
points: Vasovagal: prolonged standing, pain or emotional triggers with nausea, sweating or warmth before collapse are common.
Cardiac: arrhythmia or structural disease may produce sudden or exertional collapse, but absence of a prodrome is not obligatory.
Orthostatic: symptoms often follow standing; assess hydration, medicines and autonomic causes.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: Seizure is a transient-loss-of-consciousness mimic, not simply another mechanism of circulatory syncope.
A normal initial ECG cannot exclude every intermittent arrhythmia.

quickRevision: Vasovagal syncope often has a recognizable trigger and prodrome, while exertional or supine syncope raises cardiac concern.
Orthostatic symptoms follow standing and may reflect medication effects, dehydration or autonomic dysfunction.
Seizure, hypoglycemia and other causes can mimic syncope; recovery history helps with differentiation.

quiz.question: Which feature raises concern for cardiac rather than uncomplicated vasovagal syncope?
quiz.explanation: Syncope during exertion raises concern for structural heart disease or a rhythm disturbance and needs cardiac assessment, unlike many typical vasovagal episodes with a clear trigger and prodrome.
